scope.completion: Initial 95–237 pass extended to all effective Contracts noncase records at the release agent’s request.

method: Read all summary, notes and sections in all 331 effective records, including substantive learning-route prose. Exact repeated learning.definition/explanation values were read once in the visible prose; metadata/IDs were inspected as context. Screened for unsupported categorical rules, conflated procedural outcomes, unqualified historical or jurisdictional law, invented hypothetical answers, source-boundary overclaims and semantic repetition. Composed guarded consolidations for all 45 detected plain-prefix/original-note repetition patterns, plus the duplicated Owen source boundary.
limits: This is systematic prose screening and consolidation, not a fresh comparison of every record against its full source opinion or textbook PDF.
No complete current-law survey or fresh independent legal-merits verification of every case is claimed. Historical, jurisdictional, procedural and assigned-page qualifications are retained.

Six final formal-rule records (325–330) were read in the supplied pre-correction pack. Their identified source corrections are separately recorded by the release agent in contracts-explanation-corrections.json; they are not counted as new findings here.
Per-record fingerprints identify the effective input prose screened. Release corrections intentionally change those values, rather than silently replacing this review evidence.

findings.reason: Combine the plain-language prefix and legacy study note, preserving distinct examples, qualifications, source boundaries and analysis. This is prose consolidation, not new legal doctrine.
findings.old:
Start by identifying the exact commitment and who made it. Then identify the governing law, the parties’ agreement, and a recognized basis for enforcing the promise. In the common-law materials, consideration and promissory estoppel supply different possible bases. A writing requirement, a defect in bargaining, or public policy can still prevent enforcement. A promise may also exist even when the requested remedy, such as an order to perform, is unavailable. The course therefore separates the existence of a commitment, the grounds for enforcing it, and the consequences of breach.

Restatement § 1 supplies the introductory definition. A promise and an enforceable contract are separate steps in analysis. Common-law decisions, statutes, and persuasive restatements have different authority. Article 2 governs the sales setting within its scope, with ordinary law supplementing it unless displaced. The text begins with why enforcement occurs and what breach remedies do before turning to formation. The authors do not treat one philosophical account as the entire law.
findings.new:
Identify the exact commitment, its maker, and the governing law. Common-law decisions, enacted statutes, and persuasive restatements have different authority; Article 2 governs within its sales scope, with ordinary law supplementing it unless displaced. Consideration and promissory estoppel supply different possible grounds for enforcing a promise. A writing requirement, a defect in bargaining, or public policy can still bar enforcement, and a valid obligation does not guarantee an order to perform.

Restatement § 1 supplies the introductory definition. The course separates identifying a promise, establishing its enforceability, and choosing a remedy. It introduces reasons for enforcement and breach remedies before formation, without treating one philosophical account as the entire law.

In Hawkins, the doctor’s specific guarantee and repeated solicitation of the operation could support a finding of commitment, while estimates of the recovery period remained predictions. In Bayliner, the performance figures described a differently equipped boat, and the advertising praise did not promise a particular speed. Ask what a reasonable recipient could understand the speaker to have undertaken, and identify the evidence supporting that understanding.

Hawkins distinguishes an asserted guarantee from estimates of recovery time. Bayliner distinguishes a performance description of another configuration and general promotional praise from a warranty about the goods sold. A statement’s specificity, its relation to the actual subject, and its place in the transaction matter. A disappointing outcome alone does not establish a promise. The textbook’s theories of promise then ask why a sufficiently identified assurance should receive legal enforcement.

In Hawkins, the doctor’s specific guarantee and repeated solicitation could support a commitment, while estimates of recovery time remained predictions. In Bayliner, performance figures concerned a differently equipped boat and promotional praise did not warrant a particular speed. Specificity, connection to the actual subject, and place in the transaction matter. A disappointing result alone does not establish a promise; identify what a reasonable recipient understood the speaker to undertake and the supporting evidence. Promissory estoppel is a possible basis of liability; reliance is a possible measure of recovery. A claim’s doctrinal basis does not by itself settle the measure or permit double recovery of the same loss.

The comparison is with the position before the induced change, including provable opportunities forgone. Reliance is both an interest relevant to remedy and a component of promissory estoppel, but those functions must be kept separate. A claimant must connect the change to the assurance. In D&G Stout, the lost opportunity to sell on favorable terms differs from hoped-for future distributorship profits. Hayes asks whether a retirement decision already made before the pension promise can count as induced reliance.

D&G Stout concerns a lost opportunity to sell the business, distinct from hoped-for distributorship profits; Sullivan concerns expenses and physical or emotional injury associated with surgery. Hayes asks whether retirement decided before a pension promise was actually induced by it.

Promissory estoppel is a possible basis of liability; reliance is also a possible measure of relief. Connect the change to the assurance. The doctrinal basis alone does not settle the amount or permit recovery twice for the same loss.

The assigned cases examine whether money would adequately compensate the injured party and whether a court can administer the requested order. Morris concerns a specially trained horse, Klein an aircraft for which substitutes were available, and Walgreen a lease restriction whose violation would cause difficult-to-measure competitive loss. The remedy depends on the transaction and equitable considerations; an enforceable contract does not automatically entitle its claimant to specific relief.

Morris uses the particular trained horse’s value to the plaintiff. The notes extend the inquiry to affection for a pet and the inability to obtain sufficient tomatoes at the needed time for a cannery. Uniqueness is relevant through difficulty of substitution, not only through a category label. Personal services present different concerns; a negative injunction against competing performance is distinct from an affirmative order to render services.
findings.new:
The assigned cases ask whether damages adequately protect the claimant and whether the requested order can be administered. Morris concerns a horse the claimant personally trained; Klein concerns an aircraft with available substitutes; Walgreen concerns difficult-to-measure competitive injury from violating a lease restriction. The notes compare attachment to a pet and a cannery’s inability to obtain enough tomatoes in time. Uniqueness matters through difficulty of substitution, not merely a category label.

Specific relief depends on the transaction and equitable considerations. An enforceable contract does not automatically entitle its claimant to it. Personal services raise distinct concerns: restraining competing performance differs from affirmatively compelling service.

Identify each side of the exchange separately: what did this promisor seek, and what did the other party provide or promise in return? A performance can include an act, refraining from an act, or changing a legal relationship. Hamer illustrates requested forbearance from conduct the nephew had a legal right to pursue. Feinberg illustrates why past work and continued work that the employer did not require in exchange do not necessarily support a pension promise. The fact that a promise caused someone to act is relevant to reliance, but the consideration inquiry additionally asks whether the parties exchanged the act for the promise.

A detriment or benefit can identify a thing exchanged, but neither establishes the bargain without reciprocal inducement. Hamer involves a requested relinquishment of legal freedoms. Dyer considers forbearance of a disputed claim. Past conduct not sought in exchange for the later assurance fails the ordinary bargain analysis in Feinberg. An inducement may coexist with generosity or other motives. The text also distinguishes adequacy of the exchange, nominal recitals, and formal substitutes.
findings.new:
Identify what each promisor sought and what the other party gave or promised in exchange. The return may be an act, forbearance, or a change in a legal relationship. Hamer concerns requested surrender of lawful freedoms; Dyer concerns forbearance of a disputed claim. A benefit or detriment identifies a possible object of exchange, but reciprocal inducement is still required.

In Feinberg, past work and continued work not required as the pension’s price did not establish the bargain. Action caused by a promise may instead support reliance. Generosity or other motives can coexist with an exchange; adequacy, nominal recitals, and formal substitutes present separate questions.

findings.old:
A court’s usual refusal to compare economic values does not turn a sham exchange into consideration. The casebook contrasts a genuinely desired item of slight value with a token transfer used merely to disguise a gift. It also distinguishes the consideration inquiry from other grounds for examining an unfair bargain, including public policy and unconscionability. When explaining a problem, state whether the alleged defect concerns lack of exchange, unequal value, or a separate limitation on enforcement.

The notes place Restatement § 79’s treatment of adequacy alongside the requirement of a genuine exchange under § 71. A token amount may be part of an actual bargain, but a recital masking a gift creates a distinct question. The first and second Restatements’ examples illustrate that the formal presence of a dollar is not a complete analysis. Public-gift restrictions discussed by the editors raise additional constitutional questions that ordinary consideration doctrine alone does not resolve.
findings.new:
Restatement § 79 separates the value of an exchange from its existence under § 71. A genuinely desired item of slight value may be consideration; a token transfer or recital masking a gift raises the distinct question whether there was any real exchange. The first and second Restatements’ nominal-dollar examples prevent treating form alone as decisive.

Unequal value, lack of exchange, unconscionability, and public policy are different objections. Public-gift restrictions discussed in the notes also raise constitutional questions that ordinary consideration doctrine does not resolve.

The readings ask whether the promise and the requested return were given in exchange for each other; they do not require the exchange to be either party’s only motive. This distinction also prevents every beneficial consequence of a promise from being treated as consideration.

The text’s discussion of Restatement § 81 and Holmes’s reciprocal inducement formulation distinguishes why a party desires an outcome from the act requested as its price. A promise made partly from affection may remain bargained for. Conversely, reliance or a benefit occurring without being sought in exchange does not become consideration merely because it helps explain the transaction.

Restatement § 81 and Holmes’s reciprocal-inducement formulation distinguish why a party desires an outcome from what it requests as the price. Someone may paint for money while also seeking reputation, enjoyment, or friendship. Affection or generosity can likewise coexist with a bargain; exchange need not be either party’s only motive.

A benefit or induced act not sought in exchange does not become consideration merely because it helps explain the transaction. Identify the agreed return rather than every consequence of the promise.

The casebook also records jurisdictions using more demanding formulations. Identify what claim was surrendered, what was promised for that surrender, and what the claimant believed at the time. Dyer uses Restatement § 74 to distinguish doubt about a claim from honest belief in a claim that proves invalid. The policy of encouraging settlements does not protect knowingly baseless demands. Fiege supplies a paternity-claim comparison, while the notes ask how litigation certification duties and other legal limits bear on promises not to sue. Settlement of uncertainty is itself a bargained-for benefit, but a court must still determine what was promised and surrendered.

Restatement § 74 distinguishes doubt about a claim from honest belief in a claim that proves invalid. The casebook records more demanding formulations in other jurisdictions.

Identify the surrendered claim, the promised return, and the claimant’s belief when bargaining. Fiege supplies a paternity comparison. Settlement policy does not protect knowingly baseless harassment, and litigation certification duties or other limits may apply separately.

findings.old:
The question is what obligation the language, context, and applicable law actually impose. In Mattei, an honest judgment about satisfactory leases constrained the purchaser. In Structural Polymer, good faith and the agreed supply arrangement constrained the buyer’s requirements. In Wood, the exclusive arrangement and revenue-sharing terms supported an implied obligation to use reasonable efforts. A conditional or flexible obligation can therefore be a genuine commitment. Identify the limit on the party’s choice rather than assuming that any discretion destroys a contract.

Mattei supplies a good-faith limit on satisfaction; Structural Polymer constrains quantity through good-faith requirements and its price mechanism; Wood finds a reasonable-efforts undertaking in the whole agreement. Interpretation determines whether discretion is actually unbounded. A condition, a termination right, or an unspecified quantity should therefore be analyzed in operation rather than labeled illusory without examining its limits.
findings.new:
Examine the obligation imposed by the language, context, and governing law. Mattei limits satisfaction by honest judgment; Structural Polymer constrains requirements through good faith and the supply/price-matching arrangement; Wood implies reasonable efforts from exclusivity and revenue sharing. A conditional or flexible obligation can therefore supply a real commitment.

Identify the limit on choice before calling a promise illusory. A termination right, condition, or uncertain quantity does not automatically leave the maker free to perform nothing.

The distinction concerns the standard governing discretion and does not make all commercial decisions objectively reviewable.

Evaluating proposed leases involved rent, tenant quality, duration, restrictions, and other interdependent business considerations; dissatisfaction with them differed from regretting the purchase price. Identify the subject of satisfaction and the standard the decision actually applies. The distinction does not make every commercial judgment objectively reviewable.

Traditional equitable estoppel often concerns a representation about an existing fact; promissory estoppel concerns a commitment about future conduct. Ricketts uses the older terminology while enforcing a future promise after the granddaughter changed her position. Northrop compares three approaches: removing both conflicting clauses and using supplementary law; retaining the offeror’s clause; and treating the response’s clause like an additional term under subsection (2). The court predicts that Illinois would use the first approach, despite preferring the third as a policy matter. Its result therefore depends on the governing jurisdiction and the formation analysis. Do not describe the preferred view as the rule the court applied.

Northrop canvasses knockout of both conflicting terms, retention of the offeror’s term after dropping the offeree’s, and treatment of different terms as additional terms under a materiality analysis. The court applies the first as its prediction of Illinois law, despite a stated preference for the third. Do not infer that the alternative preferred in dicta was the rule applied or that the buyer’s more generous warranty survived the knockout.
findings.new:
Northrop compares knocking out both conflicting clauses, retaining the offeror’s clause after dropping the offeree’s, and treating the response’s clause as an additional term under subsection (2). It predicts Illinois would use the first despite preferring the third. The buyer’s more generous warranty therefore did not survive the knockout.

The applied rule depends on jurisdiction and the formation analysis. Do not mistake the court’s policy preference for its holding.

Northrop applies this approach to conflicting warranty periods in a contract recognized despite nonmatching communications. C. Itoh reaches a contract-by-conduct analysis under § 2-207(3), whose own text limits the contract to agreed terms and supplementary provisions. The two routes can resemble each other in result while arising from different statutory questions. Identify the route, identify the clauses excluded, and identify the actual source that fills the gap.

C. Itoh’s subsection (3) contract includes agreed terms plus applicable supplementary provisions; its rejected arbitration clause cannot return as a gap-filler. Northrop’s knockout of different terms in a subsection (1) setting is a separate interpretive issue. The similar practical result should not obscure the distinct statutory routes. The notes ask whether Code defaults are neutral and how those defaults shape drafting incentives.
findings.new:
Northrop’s treatment of conflicting terms in a subsection (1) contract is an interpretive issue distinct from C. Itoh’s subsection (3) contract by conduct. The latter’s text supplies agreed terms plus applicable supplementary law; an unagreed arbitration clause cannot return as a supposed gap-filler.

Identify the formation route, excluded clauses, and actual source filling each gap. The notes also ask whether Code defaults are neutral and how they influence drafting incentives.

findings.reason: Combine the plain-language prefix and legacy study note, preserving distinct examples, qualifications, source boundaries and analysis. This is prose consolidation, not new legal doctrine.
findings.old:
Hill accepts that account of the transaction and treats retention beyond the specified period as acceptance. Klocek instead treats the consumer as having made an offer that the seller already accepted, so the box terms require a separate basis for inclusion. The disagreement concerns who made the offer, when the contract formed, what notice was provided, and whether § 2-207 applies. A return period is a relevant fact; it does not automatically resolve every transaction involving later terms.

Hill uses retention after a review-and-return period to complete the vendor’s offer and treats the one-form transaction outside § 2-207. Klocek finds no textual two-form prerequisite and, on its evidentiary record, assumes the consumer made the offer and the vendor accepted earlier. The differences include governing law, procedural posture, notice, and offeror identity as well as the length of the return period.
findings.new:
Hill treats retention beyond a review-and-return period as acceptance of the vendor’s package offer and puts its one-form transaction outside § 2-207. Klocek rejects a textual two-form prerequisite and assumes on its record that the consumer offered and the vendor accepted earlier, making later terms proposals requiring agreement.

The cases differ in governing law, procedural posture, notice, offeror identity, and formation timing as well as the return period. That period is relevant, but it does not resolve every later-terms transaction.

findings.reason: Combine the plain-language prefix and legacy study note, preserving distinct examples, qualifications, source boundaries and analysis. This is prose consolidation, not new legal doctrine.
findings.old:
Specht, Dorton, C. Itoh, Hill, Klocek, and Anderson reach this question through different transaction structures. Some concern whether notice and conduct establish assent; others concern whether an additional term entered an existing contract. Graham separately examines an arbitration arrangement for unfairness even where the provision was expected. Agreement, scope, enforceability, and the particular procedural request are distinct questions.

Specht concerns notice and manifestation; Dorton asks whether arbitration was already agreed or a material added term; C. Itoh excludes it from a conduct-based contract; Hill and Klocek disagree about later terms. These decisions do not decide the underlying claims simply by resolving the forum question. Each opinion’s applicable law and evidentiary posture determine how agreement is assessed.
findings.new:
Specht examines notice and manifested assent; Dorton whether arbitration was agreed or materially added; C. Itoh its exclusion from a conduct contract; Hill and Klocek competing accounts of later terms; and Anderson attempted adoption of changed terms. Graham separately examines unfairness despite an expected arbitration arrangement.

Identify agreement, scope, enforceability, and the procedural request separately, with the applicable law and evidentiary posture. Resolving arbitration does not itself decide the underlying merits.

findings.reason: Combine the plain-language prefix and legacy study note, preserving distinct examples, qualifications, source boundaries and analysis. This is prose consolidation, not new legal doctrine.
findings.old:
The casebook’s sequence is to identify the contract, determine whether it falls within a writing requirement, examine the record’s form and content, and consider an applicable exception. Tolosa applies a Texas loan-agreement statute to a claimed promise to delay foreclosure and rejects the particular promissory-estoppel allegations. That jurisdiction-specific result should not be generalized to all oral promises. The CISG’s Article 11 supplies a contrasting approach in the assigned international materials.

Work through the particular statute: the class of agreement covered, the writing needed, whose signature is required, and any exception or defense issue. The chapter distinguishes unenforceability from absence of a contract and explores waiver and other legal uses of the agreement. Tolosa supplies a particular Texas loan provision, rather than a universal six-category rule. The historical English categories and modern state comparisons illustrate variation. The full later units on satisfaction and exceptions have not yet been assigned.
findings.new:
Identify the agreement, the governing statute’s coverage, the record’s content and form, whose signature is needed, and any exception or defense. A writing barrier differs from absence of agreement; waiver and other uses of the agreement may matter.

Tolosa applies Texas’s loan-agreement provision to delaying foreclosure and rejects the pleaded estoppel theory. It supplies no universal rule for oral promises. The historical English categories and modern state comparisons demonstrate variation; CISG Article 11 supplies a different form rule within its own scope. The full later units on satisfying writing requirements and exceptions are outside the early assigned ranges.
